statement.p: Calculate the following integral: \int x \cos(-7 x) \, dx

hint.p: We pick u and dv so that dv can be integrated, while ideally, u gets simpler.
Both x and \cos\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right) can be integrated, so we can choose for u to get simpler.

The derivative of x is 1 (which is of lower degree) while the derivative of \cos\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right) is + 7 \sin(-7 x), (which is another trig function and not any simpler). Thus, we should let u=x and dv=\cos\mathopen{}\left(-7x\right)dx.

Next, remember that the integration by parts formula says that \int u \, dv = u\cdot v - \int v \, du So, substituting in what we already know are u, \ v,\ du and dv, we get that \int x \cos(-7 x) \, dx = x \cdot \frac{1}{-7}\sin(-7 x) - \int \frac{1}{-7}\sin(-7 x) \, dx
Lastly, we integrate the second part, so the answer is \int x \cos(-7 x) \, dx = \frac{1}{-7} x \sin(-7 x) + \frac{1}{49}\cos(-7 x)+C

solution.p: The integration by parts formula says that \int u \, dv = u\cdot v - \int v \, du So, substituting in, we get that \int x \cos(-7 x) \, dx = x \cdot \frac{1}{-7}\sin(-7 x - \int \frac{1}{-7}\sin(-7 x) \cdot dx Lastly, we integrate the second part, so the answer is \int x \cos(-7 x) \, dx = \frac{1}{-7} x \sin(-7 x) + \frac{1}{49}\cos(-7 x)+C
